Senses.Explanation: The twelve periods are the traditional double-hours that together span a complete day and night. Huangbo Xiyun speaks of relying on nothing throughout them; Xitang Zhizang asks the same all-day question in two parallel transmissions; an unnamed monk puts it to Fayan Wenyi; Maqiaoshan Benkong and Fenyang Shanzhao use the span in their own addresses. Huanji comments on the phrase while discussing Baozhi. A biographical title meaning “Twelve-Hour Song” is not evidence for this standalone sense and has been excluded. The phrase means the whole day, not twelve modern sixty-minute hours.

Senses.Explanation: The expression denotes the Ten Oxen in these Chan records. Its wording is "ten oxen." As a Chan title and label, it denotes Liangshan Kuoan's ordered set of ox-herding verses and the pictures made from them. A collection titles the work "Liangshan Kuoan Ze's Ten-Ox Verses" (梁山廓庵則和尚十牛頌); another record says, "our school has the account of herding the ox, and Liangshan has the verses on the Ten Oxen" (我宗門有牧牛之說，梁山有十牛之頌). The sequence begins with named sections including "seeking the ox" (尋牛) and "seeing the tracks" (見跡). The corpus also records direct criticism of its later handling: Baichi calls Liangshan's verses "compassionate, talk that descends into the weeds" (慈悲之故，落草之談), says later people "made a wrong move and then painted these Ten-Ox forms" (錯下手腳，更畫此十牛樣子), and urges burning them. In an encounter, the identified teacher interrupts the recorded questioner asked to recite the verses and asks, "Where is the ox?" (牛在甚麼處). The deviation from an ordinary count of cattle is documentary: "the Ten Oxen" (十牛) functions as the proper name of a Chan verse-and-picture series, circulated, recited, questioned, and criticized inside the record.

This deictic expression points back to a just-demonstrated action, wording, interpretation, or state: “in this way,” “like this,” or simply “so.” Huineng asks what is coming “in this way”; Shitou Xiqian blocks “this way,” “not this way,” and both together; Yuanwu Keqin warns that understanding in this way misses the matter, but elsewhere says that seeing in this way gives a share of freedom. The phrase also forms recurrent frames: “at precisely such a time” (正當恁麼時), “if so” (恁麼則), “must be this way” (直須恁麼), and Yuanwu Keqin’s self-reference to “talking this way” (恁麼說話). Foyan Qingyuan juxtaposes repeated “this way” with repeated “not this way,” while Sixin Wuxin says a great man is not made this way. Its translation therefore follows the demonstrative relation in each turn; the word does not itself name a teaching or a single approved manner.

Senses.Explanation: “If so, then” is the student’s recurrent inference formula in public exchanges, immediately tested or overturned by the recorded reply. A conversational connective: 'being so' followed by 'then,' hence 'if so, then.' It occurs 5,426 times in 317 allowlisted texts. Chan encounter records give it a conspicuous turn-taking role: a questioner repeats or draws an inference from a respondent's answer, and that respondent may confirm, reverse, test, or reject the inference. Recorded replies call the inference wild talk, reverse its premise, block it with an image, ask for the student's own part, or demand how the claimed conclusion is carried out. These outcomes are deployments of the same connective, not new senses. Its distinctive role is the recurrent public-interview hinge where a proposed understanding becomes answerable to the next line.
